extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, journalists, students and scholars of news communication and content analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Galtung & Ruge's 1965 factors that determine which world events become foreign news in newspapers (i.e., operationalizing 'newsworthiness' for content analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 'frequency' of an event we refer to the time-span needed for the event to unfold itself and acquire meaning. The more similar the frequency of the event is to the frequency of the news medium, the more probable that it will be recorded as news by that news medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daily newspapers favor events that unfold within their publication interval (e.g., a single murder can be reported next day; long-term developments usually go unreported unless they reach a dramatic climax such as an inauguration). Publications with lower frequency (weeklies, monthlies) can correct under-reporting of long-term trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amplitude / Absolute intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: The stronger the signal, the greater the amplitude, the more probable that it will be recorded as worth listening to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is effectively a threshold of size/severity: larger events (bigger dam, more violent murder) are more likely to be reported, other things equal. The concept can be used dichotomously: event must pass a threshold before being recorded as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity increase (change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that show an increase in intensity (a striking change or escalation) are more likely to be recorded as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change or sudden escalation can make otherwise moderate events newsworthy (e.g., increasing violence, sudden breakthroughs). The text contrasts absolute intensity with intensity increase as separate contributing factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity (clarity of signal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more clear and unambiguous the signal (the less noise there is), the more probable that it will be recorded as worth listening to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events with a single or limited interpretation are preferred to highly ambiguous events. Clarity here refers to interpretability and one-dimensionality (easy to present and understand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The more meaningful the signal, the more probable that it will be recorded as worth listening to; 'meaningful' includes interpretability within the cultural framework of the listener/reader and relevance (what it implies for the reader).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaning includes cultural proximity (ethnocentrism) — culturally similar events are noticed more readily — and relevance (an event in a distant country can still be meaningful if it implies consequences for the reader's group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance with pre-image / expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The more consonant the signal is with the mental image of what one expects to find, the more probable that it will be recorded as worth listening to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consonance can be cognitive ('predicts') or normative ('wants'); news are often 'olds' because they correspond to expectations. Excessively dissonant events may be ignored unless other factors intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness (rarity / novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more unexpected the signal, the more probable that it will be recorded as worth listening to — particularly the unexpected within the meaningful and consonant set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected/rare occurrences attract attention more than regular/institutionalized matters. News tends to report the unexpected or rare rather than steady, repetitive processes (e.g., disasters over routine progress).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity / inertia (persistence after selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once something has hit the headlines and been defined as 'news', then it will continue to be defined as news for some time even if amplitude is reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A channel once opened tends to stay open due to system inertia and because the unexpected becomes familiar; initial selection increases subsequent coverage (feed-forward amplification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition / desire for a balanced presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of a news programme/page (need for variety and balance) affects thresholds: presence of many items of a type raises threshold for new items of that type, while presence of other kinds lowers threshold for including diverse items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors aim to present a 'balanced' whole; e.g., adding minor domestic news may lower threshold for a foreign piece of a different kind so the broadcast/newspaper appears balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite nations
rubrics_metrics.description: The more the event concerns elite nations, the more probable that it will become a news item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News is elite-centered geographically: events involving powerful or 'topdog' nations receive disproportionate attention because actions of elites/nations are seen as more consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite people
rubrics_metrics.description: The more the event concerns elite people, the more probable that it will become a news item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elite individuals serve as objects of identification and representation; stories about elites can stand in for broader social narratives and thus are preferentially reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification (reference to persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more the event can be seen in personal terms, as due to the action of specific individuals, the more probable that it will become a news item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News tends to present events with named subjects (persons) rather than structural/social forces. The authors offer five explanations: cultural idealism (man-as-agent), need for identification, fit with media frequency, connection to elite concentration, and technical ease (photos/interviews). Personification reduces complexity and aids reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativization (reference to negative consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more negative the event in its consequences, the more probable that it will become a news item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative news is preferred for multiple reasons: (1) it often satisfies the frequency criterion (negativity unfolds quickly), (2) tends to be more consensual/unambiguous in interpretation, (3) may be consonant with dominant pre-images (e.g., anxiety), and (4) is often more unexpected. These mechanisms explain the prevalence of negative reporting.
